alternatives: Levonorgestrel intrauterine system: UKMEC 2; also reduces dysmenorrhoea and menstrual bleeding

contraindications: Migraine with aura, at any age and at any ethinylestradiol dose (20 micrograms included): UKMEC category 4 and WHO MEC category 4 (unacceptable health risk) for all combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch, ring) (UKMEC 2025; WHO MEC 5th edition 2015).
interactions: Rizatriptan and ibuprofen (current): no clinically relevant interaction with combined oral contraceptives.
Lamotrigine: ethinylestradiol lowers lamotrigine levels; relevant only if both are taken.
output.summary: Low-dose ethinylestradiol does not change the category: combined contraception is category 4 with aura; the levonorgestrel IUS also treats dysmenorrhoea.
warnings: Switch without a gap in contraceptive cover.
Topiramate at 200 mg a day or more reduces the efficacy of oral hormonal contraception, including the progestogen-only pill.

contraindications: Propranolol: asthma, second- or third-degree heart block, marked bradycardia.
interactions: Propranolol with rizatriptan: propranolol raises rizatriptan exposure by about 70%; use rizatriptan 5 mg, taken at least 2 hours after propranolol, maximum 3 doses in 24 hours (rizatriptan label).
Candesartan, amitriptyline, lamotrigine, topiramate: no pharmacokinetic interaction with rizatriptan.
Topiramate with oral hormonal contraception: reduced contraceptive efficacy at 200 mg a day or more.
output.proposed: Migraine preventive with current rizatriptan 10 mg: propranolol, candesartan, amitriptyline, lamotrigine, topiramate
output.summary: With propranolol, rizatriptan must drop to 5 mg; topiramate and candesartan need reliable contraception.
warnings: Topiramate is teratogenic: use only under a pregnancy prevention programme with highly effective contraception (MHRA 2024).
Lamotrigine: titrate slowly (25 mg daily for 2 weeks, then 50 mg) to reduce the risk of serious rash.
Sodium valproate: not for women who can become pregnant unless a pregnancy prevention programme applies.

output.query: migraine aura longer than 60 minutes classification and preventive treatment

results.finding: Migraine with aura needs only three of six aura characteristics, so an aura lasting over 60 minutes can still be 1.2.1. Persistent aura without infarction (1.4.2) requires aura symptoms persisting for at least 1 week; migrainous infarction (1.4.3) requires an aura symptom lasting over 60 minutes with neuroimaging showing ischaemic infarction in the relevant area.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211 (1.2, 1.4.2, 1.4.3)

results.finding: In an open-label study of people with migraine with aura, lamotrigine reduced the frequency and duration of aura.
results.source: Lampl C et al. Lamotrigine reduces migraine aura and migraine attacks in patients with migraine with aura. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2005;76:1730-1732

output.summary: Aura over 60 minutes without infarct remains migraine with aura; prevention is considered for prolonged aura, and lamotrigine has open-label evidence for reducing aura.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Three attacks in 8 months of unilateral positive spreading visual aura lasting 30, 50 and 70-75 minutes, each followed by migrainous headache: 4 of 6 C characteristics with the duration criterion failed in the last attack; normal examination; prolonged and lengthening aura are red flags
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with examination and apply ICHD-3 1.2 criteria A to D
action_criteria.rationale: The history decides that the attacks are migraine with typical aura despite one aura over 60 minutes (3 of 6 suffice), and identifies the prolonged aura as the red flag for imaging and a reason to consider prevention.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct in the occipital cortex on DWI or FLAIR three weeks after the 70-75 minute aura; single punctate non-specific subcortical hyperintensity
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI for an aura lasting over 60 minutes
action_criteria.rationale: An aura lasting over 60 minutes raises migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.3), which needs an infarct on imaging; at three weeks an infarct would still show on FLAIR. MRI is preferred to CT (Evans RW et al., Headache 2020;60:318-336; AAN 2000).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Gedarel 20 identified as category 4 under UKMEC and WHO MEC despite the 20 microgram dose, with the levonorgestrel IUS and other progestogen-only methods as options
action_criteria.label: Check her low-dose combined oral contraceptive (Gedarel 20) against migraine with aura
action_criteria.rationale: She takes an oestrogen-containing pill; combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC 2025 and WHO MEC 2015 category 4 in migraine with aura at any oestrogen dose, so the check changes management.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Rizatriptan 5 mg if propranolol is chosen; topiramate and candesartan need reliable contraception
action_criteria.label: Check the chosen preventive against her rizatriptan
action_criteria.rationale: Prevention is being considered while she takes rizatriptan 10 mg; propranolol requires the rizatriptan dose to be halved (label).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on the classification of aura over 60 minutes and on prevention
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on prolonged migraine aura
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; the diagnosis rests on the history and the MRI.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
Do not offer sodium valproate for prevention: she can become pregnant and valproate is restricted to use under a pregnancy prevention programme when nothing else works (MHRA).
required_recommendations: Stop Gedarel 20 now: combined hormonal contraception is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura whatever the oestrogen dose; switch without a gap, preferably to a levonorgestrel IUS, which also treats her dysmenorrhoea, or to a progestogen-only pill, implant or copper IUD.
Counsel to take rizatriptan at headache onset, not during the aura, where it does not work; it may be combined with ibuprofen or naproxen.

Offer prevention because the aura is lengthening and has exceeded 60 minutes (AHS 2021): for example propranolol 80-160 mg a day (then rizatriptan 5 mg), candesartan 8-16 mg a day (only with reliable contraception, as it is contraindicated in pregnancy), or lamotrigine titrated slowly for aura-predominant attacks; review with a headache diary at 8-12 weeks.

If topiramate is chosen, start it only with highly effective contraception (copper or hormonal IUD, or implant) under the topiramate pregnancy prevention programme; it reduces the efficacy of oral and progestogen-only pills.
Advise urgent assessment if an aura lasts longer than usual or any symptom has not resolved after an hour, because migrainous infarction must then be excluded.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis; neither is present here

Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura without stroke; PFO closure does not treat migraine (PREMIUM, Tobis JM et al., JACC 2017; PRIMA, Mattle HP et al., Eur Heart J 2016; MIST, Dowson A et al., Circulation 2008).
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; no role unless cardioembolic stroke is on the differential

accepted: Migraine with prolonged aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1, aura >60 min in some attacks); combined OCP contraindicated; migrainous infarction excluded by normal DWI; preventive therapy required

differential.key_features: Needs an aura symptom over 60 minutes with an infarct in the relevant area; MRI three weeks after the 70-75 minute right-field aura shows a normal left occipital cortex on DWI and FLAIR.
Requires aura symptoms persisting for at least 1 week; her aura resolved within 75 minutes.
Positive, expanding zigzag arc followed by migrainous headache, recurring in a 31-year-old non-smoker without vascular risk factors; MRI shows no infarct.

Occipital seizures give brief coloured circular phenomena lasting seconds to a few minutes; her zigzag arc expands over 30-75 minutes and is followed by a migrainous headache; occipital lobes normal on MRI.

differential.diagnosis: Occipital AVM or other structural lesion
differential.key_features: Fully reversible attacks with a following migrainous headache that has changed side between attacks; MRI shows no flow voids, haemorrhage or mass.

key_clinical_evidence: Three attacks in 8 months of unilateral positive spreading visual aura lasting 30, 50 and 70-75 minutes, each followed by migrainous headache: migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1; 4 of 6 C characteristics).
Migrainous infarction (ICHD-3 1.4.3) needs an infarct in the relevant area: MRI three weeks after the longest aura shows a normal occipital cortex on DWI and FLAIR.
Gedarel 20 is still combined hormonal contraception: UKMEC category 4 with aura at a 20 microgram dose; the levonorgestrel IUS also treats her dysmenorrhoea.
Lengthening aura is a reason to consider prevention (AHS 2021); if propranolol is chosen, rizatriptan drops to 5 mg.
Rizatriptan taken during the aura did not shorten it: triptans are taken at headache onset.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Migrainous infarction requires an infarct on imaging; MRI shows none, and a single aura over 60 minutes is compatible with migraine with typical aura.
red_herrings.data_point: Aura lasting 70-75 minutes in the most recent attack

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: UKMEC and WHO MEC category 4 applies to all combined hormonal contraception with aura, whatever the oestrogen dose.
red_herrings.intended_effect: A 20 microgram pill may be assumed to be acceptable

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A punctate frontal hyperintensity is non-specific, common in migraine with aura, and not in the occipital territory of her aura.
red_herrings.data_point: Single punctate frontal subcortical white matter hyperintensity on MRI
red_herrings.intended_effect: May be read as a small infarct

sequence_constraints.reason: The structured history identifies the red flag (aura over 60 minutes) that justifies imaging.

findings.result: Three attacks in 8 months (8 months, 4 months and 3 weeks ago); no migraine or aura before.
Visual only: a shimmering zigzag arc that pulsates and expands; in the last attack in the right visual field. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptom. Fully reversible; vision normal since.
The arc expands gradually across the field.
About 30, 50 and 70-75 minutes in successive attacks; the most recent exceeded 60 minutes.
Severe throbbing headache (8-9/10) after each aura resolves, right-sided in the first attack and left-sided in the last, with nausea and photophobia, lasting 10-14 hours.
Rizatriptan 10 mg wafer taken during the last aura: the aura did not shorten; the headache was less severe. Ibuprofen 400-600 mg as needed.

Headache-free. Visual fields full, no papilloedema, eye movements normal, power 5/5 without drift, sensation intact, reflexes 2+ and symmetric, plantars flexor, coordination and gait normal. BP 116/74 mmHg.

Aura lasting over 60 minutes, recent onset (8 months) and lengthening aura with each attack: present. Systemic symptoms, history of neoplasm, persisting deficit, thunderclap onset, age over 50, positional or Valsalva trigger, papilloedema, pregnancy, painful eye, head trauma, immune suppression and analgesic overuse: absent.
Combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol 20 micrograms with desogestrel 150 micrograms) for dysmenorrhoea and contraception. Non-smoker; no hypertension or diabetes.

clinical_assessment.impression:
1. Three attacks of unilateral, positive, spreading visual aura followed by migrainous headache: ICHD-3 1.2 met (4 of 6 C characteristics; the duration criterion not met in the last attack, 70-75 minutes). Supports migraine with typical aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) with one prolonged aura.
2. Aura fully resolved with a normal examination: no persisting symptom to suggest persistent aura or infarction.
3. Red flags present: aura over 60 minutes, recent onset, lengthening aura.

scores.ICHD-3 criterion C characteristics met: 4 of 6 (at least 3 required): spread, unilateral, positive, headache within 60 min; succession absent; duration over 60 min in the last attack

additional_observations: Occipital cortex and optic radiations normal on DWI, ADC, T2 and FLAIR; no cortical signal change or gliosis.
No haemorrhage or microhaemorrhage on susceptibility-weighted imaging.
No mass, abnormal flow voids or cortical malformation.
Ventricles, sulci and posterior fossa normal for age.
mri.impression:
1. No acute or subacute infarct, haemorrhage or structural lesion; occipital lobes normal.
2. Single punctate right frontal subcortical white matter hyperintensity, non-specific.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 31-year-old Mexican-American woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic for evaluation of three episodes of visual disturbance over the past 8 months, each involving increasingly prolonged visual aura. The first episode 8 months ago involved a classic expanding zigzag arc lasting approximately 30 minutes followed by a severe right-sided headache. The second episode 4 months ago lasted approximately 50 minutes. The most recent episode 3 weeks ago involved visual disturbance in the right visual field — a shimmering arc that she described as 'pulsating and expanding' — that lasted approximately 70-75 minutes before eventually fading. After each visual aura resolves, she develops a severe left-sided throbbing headache (8-9/10) with nausea and photophobia lasting 10-14 hours.

She is concerned about the increasing duration of her auras. She is aware that 'aura lasting more than 60 minutes' can be significant. She took a rizatriptan 10 mg wafer during the most recent visual aura to try to stop it — the aura did not shorten but the subsequent headache was less severe. She has no prior history of migraine or aura before 8 months ago. Her aunt on her maternal side is known to have migraines. She is on the combined oral contraceptive pill (Gedarel 20 — EE 20 mcg + desogestrel 150 mcg) prescribed for dysmenorrhoea. She is a non-smoker. No prior stroke or TIA. She is a healthcare assistant in a hospital, so has some medical knowledge and is seeking specific guidance.
